sysd-scale-043.title: Replication: keeping several copies in step
sysd-scale-043.text:
Keep a second copy of your data and one question follows at once: what happens when the copies disagree? Replication means maintaining multiple copies of data, processes or resources so that redundant components stay consistent. It is a fundamental technique across databases, file systems and distributed systems. It improves availability, accessibility and performance, and in databases it improves durability too.

Replication does three jobs. Systems keep operating when components fail, through {{ref:sysd-scale-058}}. They serve requests from geographically distributed locations. And they balance load across machines. Copying data across multiple nodes also scales read operations while improving redundancy. Data replication stores the same data on multiple storage devices. Computation replication runs the same task many times, either on separate devices, in space, or repeatedly on one device, in time.

Ideally users never notice. Access to a replicated entity is typically uniform with access to a single one. The switch to a replica after a failure should be hidden as much as possible. The challenge is keeping replicas consistent while managing the trade-offs between consistency, availability and partition tolerance, constraints known as the {{ref:sysd-scale-107}}. Do not confuse replication with {{ref:sysd-reliab-189}}. That copy stays unchanged for a long period, while replicas are updated frequently and quickly lose any historical state.

sysd-scale-056.title: Single point of failure: the part with no spare
sysd-scale-056.text: One part failing alone can stop everything. That is a single point of failure: a part of a system that would stop the entire system from working if it failed. No spare or redundant option exists to keep the system functioning without it, and its interruption is substantially more disruptive than an error elsewhere. So it is undesirable in any system aiming at high availability or reliability. Systems are made robust by adding redundancy at every such point, found by identifying the critical components whose malfunction would cause total failure. At the system level, one normally deploys a load balancer for a server cluster, with spare servers ready to take over. At the site level, the whole cluster may be replicated elsewhere, because a data center can itself be a single point of failure. Scholars have argued that outsourcing that duplication to cloud providers only moves the single point of failure. The Internet avoids the problem: multiple paths let packets route around the failure of any one path or node.

sysd-scale-058.title: Failover: when a standby takes over
sysd-scale-058.text:
Failover is switching to a redundant or standby computer server, system, hardware component or network when the previously active one fails or terminates abnormally. The system keeps operating, and users should notice as little as possible. How it works depends on the replication scheme.

In failover clustering, passive replica servers copy the master's data to prepare for takeover, while the master is the only server active for client interaction. In a primary-backup scheme, taken up in {{ref:sysd-scale-104}}, a standby process takes over if the primary fails. In master-slave replication, a slave is promoted to master or a new master is provisioned. In master-master replication, failover is simple, automatic and quick, because both masters already serve reads and writes.

Tools make this concrete. In PostgreSQL a standby leaves standby mode and becomes the primary when pg_ctl promote is run. A warm standby is typically only moments from full availability once activated.

Automatic failover can also be dangerous. If a primary cannot tell whether its secondary is healthy, one SRE design has it make itself unavailable and call a human, to avoid {{ref:sysd-scale-123}}. That protects data but hurts availability and scales poorly.

sysd-scale-128.title: Gossip protocols: spreading news like an epidemic
sysd-scale-128.text: In a network of 25,000 machines, a search string can reach every one of them in about 15 rounds of gossip. A gossip or epidemic protocol is a procedure of peer-to-peer communication based on the way epidemics spread. Each node periodically picks another node at random and shares what it knows. A rumor roughly doubles its reach each round, and the doubling keeps the protocol robust even when some messages are lost. That is why information reaches all nodes in time logarithmic in system size. Dissemination protocols flood information through the network with bounded worst-case load. Aggregation protocols compute network-wide values, such as the largest or smallest, with fixed-size pairwise exchanges. Gossip keeps distributed databases consistent, counts nodes, spreads news, builds overlay networks and elects leaders, and Dynamo uses a gossip-based protocol for membership and failure detection. The SRE book warns that heartbeats and gossip will always have reliability problems for master election and group membership, which are problems of {{ref:sysd-scale-008}}.

sysd-scale-044.title: Single-leader replication: one node takes every write
sysd-scale-044.text: In this design every write has exactly one destination. In single-leader replication, one database instance is the leader that handles all writes and propagates them to replica nodes. The leader logs its updates, and each replica acknowledges receipt. Replicas primarily serve reads, but they may serve stale data because of replication lag, the delay in propagating changes from the leader. In the familiar master-slave form, the master serves reads and writes and replicates writes to one or more slaves, which serve only reads. If the master goes offline, the system keeps operating in read-only mode until a slave is promoted to master or a new master is provisioned. The benefits are clear. Copying the whole database for safekeeping barely affects the master. Applications can read from slaves without loading it, and slaves can go offline and be synced back without downtime. The costs are also clear: more hardware and complexity, and downtime and possible data loss when the master fails. All writes still go to the master, and more read slaves mean more replication lag.

sysd-scale-131.title: Log shipping: a standby that replays the primary's log
sysd-scale-131.text: If the primary dies, the transactions it has not yet shipped die with it. That is the bargain of log shipping, a high-availability setup. A standby server continuously replays the primary's write-ahead log (WAL) and is ready to take over if the primary fails. The primary runs in continuous archiving mode and each standby in continuous recovery mode, reading the WAL files, so the two servers are only loosely coupled. It needs no changes to database tables, so it has low administration overhead and a relatively low performance impact on the primary. File-based shipping sends WAL one 16MB segment at a time, cheaply over any distance. Record-based shipping streams WAL changes incrementally over a network connection. Because log shipping is asynchronous, archive_timeout can shrink the loss window to a few seconds at the cost of bandwidth, and streaming replication allows a much smaller one. A standby is typically moments from full availability once activated, which makes it a warm standby. Primary and standby should be as similar as possible, in hardware architecture and major PostgreSQL version.

sysd-scale-124.title: Leader election: choosing one organizer
sysd-scale-124.text: Every node in a network must agree on a single organizer, and none may dispute it. Leader election is the process of designating a single process as the organizer of a task distributed among several nodes. A valid algorithm must terminate in finite time, ensure uniqueness (exactly one process considers itself leader) and ensure agreement (all other processes know who the leader is). The nodes must break the symmetry among them. With unique, comparable identities, they can choose the highest. No deterministic algorithm can elect a leader in an anonymous ring, where all processes are identical, because symmetry cannot be broken. In the Chang and Roberts ring algorithm each processor sends its ID clockwise, passing on bigger IDs and discarding smaller ones, so the highest ID wins. Leader election is equivalent to distributed {{ref:sysd-scale-008}}, so the SRE book recommends formally proven systems wherever you see leader election, critical shared state or distributed locking. In {{ref:sysd-scale-021}}, a follower that hears no heartbeat becomes a candidate and starts an election.

sysd-scale-045.title: Multi-master replication: every member can write
sysd-scale-045.text: What if every copy of the data could accept writes? In multi-master replication, a group of computers stores the data and any member can update it. All members respond to client queries, and the system propagates each member's changes to the other members and resolves conflicts between concurrent changes. Unlike failover clustering, where passive replicas prepare for takeover and only the master serves clients, every master is active. In master-slave replication, a single master per data item makes consistency easier to achieve but is less flexible. The main purposes are increased availability and faster server response time. If one master fails the others keep updating, and masters can sit in several physical sites, enabling local write processing across data centers. The drawbacks are real. Most systems are only loosely consistent, lazy and asynchronous. Eager replication is complex and adds latency, and conflict resolution can become intractable as nodes and latency grow. Jim Gray argued that unless data splits naturally into disjoint sub-databases, concurrency control conflicts seriously degrade performance, with slowdown possibly scaling as O(n³) in the number of replicas.

sysd-scale-046.title: When two leaders disagree: resolving replication conflicts
sysd-scale-046.text: If one record changes on two leader nodes at once, which change wins? The most common challenge in multi-master replication is exactly this. When concurrent modifications land on different leader nodes, a replicated database must either prevent the transactional conflict or resolve it afterwards. Most synchronous (eager) replication solutions prevent conflicts, while asynchronous (lazy) solutions have to resolve them. An eager system detects the conflict before confirming the commit and aborts one transaction. A lazy system lets both commit and resolves the conflict during re-synchronization. Conflict resolution methods include last-write-wins, application-specific logic and merging concurrent updates.

sysd-scale-125.title: CRDTs: data structures that merge themselves
sysd-scale-125.text: League of Legends runs in-game chat for 7.5 million concurrent users, at 11,000 messages per second, on the Riak implementation of a conflict-free replicated data type. A conflict-free replicated data type (CRDT) is a data structure replicated across computers. Any replica can update it independently and concurrently, and a built-in algorithm resolves inconsistencies so replicas converge. Uncoordinated concurrent updates can leave replicas inconsistent in ways that may not be resolvable. Optimistic replication lets all updates through and merges later, and CRDTs are the data structures for which that merge always works. They are a common way to obtain {{ref:sysd-scale-099}}, in two variants, state-based and operation-based. Their development was motivated by collaborative text editing and mobile computing, and they have also been used in online chat. Redis, Riak and Cosmos DB have CRDT data types. A sequence CRDT can build a collaborative real-time editor as an alternative to {{ref:sysd-q-145}}.

sysd-scale-047.title: Synchronous and asynchronous replication: wait or don't wait
sysd-scale-047.text:
For a 10 km distance the fastest possible round trip takes 67 μs, whereas an entire local cached write completes in about 10–20 μs. That gap is the heart of a choice every replicated system makes: does a write wait for the remote copy?

Synchronous replication waits. A write is not complete until both local and remote storage acknowledge it, so it guarantees zero data loss with atomic write operations. In a synchronous database, a transaction is not committed until all servers have committed it, so failover loses nothing. The price is performance. Most applications wait for the write to complete, so overall performance falls considerably. It drops in proportion to distance, since minimum latency is set by the speed of light. Latency decides how far apart sites can be.

Asynchronous replication does not wait. A write is complete as soon as local storage acknowledges it, and remote storage updates with a small lag. It can be near-real-time but more commonly runs on a schedule, and it is more cost-effective. Performance is much higher. But the most recent data may be lost if local storage fails, transactions might be lost in a failover, and replicas may return slightly stale results.

Semi-synchronous replication sits between the two. A write counts as complete when local storage acknowledges it and the remote server receives or logs it. The remote write itself is asynchronous, so durability is not guaranteed on local failure.

sysd-scale-122.title: Quorum: how many votes are enough
sysd-scale-122.text: Two groups cut off from each other cannot both hold a majority. That is the idea behind a quorum: the minimum number of votes a {{ref:sysd-scale-001}} must obtain before it may perform an operation in a distributed system. Quorum-based techniques enforce consistent operation, both as a replica control method and as a commit method that keeps transactions atomic despite network partitioning. In replica control each copy holds a vote, and an operation needs a read quorum Vr or a write quorum Vw. The rule Vr + Vw > V, where V is the total votes, makes every read quorum include the newest version. A second rule ensures two write operations on the same item cannot happen concurrently, and together the two rules maintain one-copy serializability. In commit protocols a transaction runs only if a majority of sites vote for it, so it cannot commit and abort at once. In a partitioned cluster, the sub-partition holding a majority of the votes stays available while the others fall into an auto-fencing mode.

sysd-scale-129.title: Leaderless replication: the Dynamo approach
sysd-scale-129.text: In this design no node is special. In leaderless replication any replica accepts writes, as in Dynamo, a set of techniques for a highly available key-value store with no distinguished node. DynamoDB, built on Dynamo's principles, uses single-leader replication instead. Dynamo's principles are symmetry, with the same responsibilities on every node, and decentralization, peer-to-peer over central control. They also include incremental scalability, adding one node at a time, and heterogeneity, with work proportional to server capability. It partitions data with {{ref:sysd-scale-078}}. For highly available writes it uses {{ref:sysd-scale-024}} and reconciles conflicting versions during reads. For temporary failures, a sloppy quorum and hinted handoff keep availability and durability when some replicas are unavailable. For permanent failures, anti-entropy with Merkle trees finds differences between replica owners so divergent replicas can be synchronized proactively. Membership and failure detection use a gossip-based protocol, which avoids a central registry and preserves symmetry. Cassandra, Project Voldemort and Riak were inspired by the Dynamo paper.

sysd-scale-049.title: The read replica pattern: writes to one, reads from many
sysd-scale-049.text: Viewing an order history changes nothing, so it does not need to touch the primary. In the read replica pattern, all data-modifying commands go to the primary database and reads go to read replicas. Inserts, deletes and updates are sent to the primary and replicated to the read replicas, which serve reads such as viewing order details or order history. There are two common ways to implement it: embed the routing logic in the application code, or use database middleware. Middleware provides transparent routing between the application and the database servers, with rules customizable by user, schema, statement and so on. It acts as a proxy using the standard MySQL network protocol. It simplifies application code, since the application need not know the database topology, and any MySQL-compatible client can connect, which makes database migration easier. The cost is complexity and network latency. Because all queries go through it, middleware usually needs a high-availability setup to avoid becoming a single point of failure.

openers.replication: Anything that exists only once can stop the whole system when it breaks. Replication answers that by maintaining multiple copies of data, processes or resources so that redundant components stay consistent. When one copy fails, failover lets a standby or replica take over so the system keeps operating. The hard part is writes: in single-leader replication one instance handles them all, while in multi-master replication any member can update, so conflicting changes must be prevented or resolved. Synchronous replication waits for the remote copy to acknowledge a write, asynchronous replication does not, and a quorum is the minimum number of votes needed before an operation may proceed.
